overview.title: Gradient normalization and the TensorFlow gradient-ascent step
overview.main_topic: Preparing the gradient-ascent step that turns an input image into the pattern a chosen Xception filter responds to most strongly: when to use model(x) versus predict(), the L2 gradient-normalization trick, and the start of the TensorFlow implementation with GradientTape and tape.watch().
overview.central_idea: To visualize a filter we maximize its mean activation with respect to the input pixels. That needs a differentiable forward pass (model(x), not predict()), a gradient whose size is kept constant by L2 normalization, and backend-level gradient machinery. In TensorFlow that machinery is a GradientTape that must be told explicitly to watch the image tensor.
overview.importance: This page links the high-level Keras workflow to the low-level autodiff APIs of the three backends. It also gives a practical rule that recurs whenever you optimize inputs instead of weights (feature visualization, DeepDream, adversarial examples, Grad-CAM): differentiate with respect to the input, and control the step size by normalizing the gradient.
learning_objectives: Explain when to call model(x) and when to call model.predict(x), and why predict() cannot be used inside a gradient loop.
Define the L2 norm of a gradient tensor and explain why dividing by it keeps the gradient-ascent updates within a stable range.
Describe the role of the feature_extractor model and the compute_loss function (mean activation of one filter, borders excluded).
Read the first part of Listing 10.11: the @tf.function decorator, the GradientTape scope and the reason for tape.watch(image).
Name the gradient APIs of the three backends: GradientTape (TensorFlow), .backward() (PyTorch), jax.grad() (JAX).
prerequisites: Gradient descent and what a gradient is (chapter 2)
TensorFlow GradientTape basics, including tape.watch() for constant tensors (p.91)
Keras functional API: building a Model from an input and an intermediate layer output
The idea of filter visualization by gradient ascent in input space (p.315)

summary:
The page opens by finishing the sidebar from p.317 on **`model.predict(x)` versus `model(x)`**. Its conclusion is practical: use `model(x)` when you need gradients of the model call, and use `predict()` when you only need output values. In other words, always use `predict()` unless you are writing a low-level gradient loop, as the authors are doing here. (On p.317 the sidebar explained why: `predict()` runs batch by batch and returns NumPy values, so it scales to large arrays but cannot be differentiated through.)

Next comes a **non-obvious trick**: before using the gradient, divide it by its **L2 norm**, the square root of the sum of the squares of all its values. The update direction stays the same, but every update to the input image now has roughly the same magnitude, so gradient ascent is not thrown off by gradients that are very large or very small.

The authors then point out that anything involving gradients requires a **backend-level API**: `GradientTape` in TensorFlow, `.backward()` in PyTorch, `jax.grad()` in JAX. They present the step function once for each backend, starting with TensorFlow in **section 10.2.1**. In TensorFlow you open a `GradientTape` scope, compute the loss inside it, and retrieve the gradients; a `@tf.function` decorator compiles the step for speed.

A recap code block collects the shared setup. It loads the Xception backbone (`xception_41_imagenet`) from KerasHub, picks the layer `block3_sepconv1`, builds a `feature_extractor` model that outputs that layer's activations, and defines `compute_loss(image, filter_index)`. That function returns the **mean activation of one filter**, computed only over spatial positions at least 2 pixels from the border.

Finally, **Listing 10.11** begins: `import tensorflow as tf`, the `@tf.function`-decorated `gradient_ascent_step(image, filter_index, learning_rate)`, a `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` block, and `tape.watch(image)`. The callout explains that the image must be watched explicitly because it is not a TensorFlow `Variable`, and only Variables are watched automatically. The rest of the listing (loss, gradient, normalization, update, return) is on p.319.

paragraphs.excerpt: You should use `model(x)` when you need to retrieve the gradients of the model call.
paragraphs.what_it_says: This ends the sidebar 'The difference between model.predict(x) and model(x)'. Use model(x) when you need gradients of the model call. Use predict() when you only need the output values. Always use predict() unless you are inside a low-level gradient-descent loop, which is the situation in this section.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two calls compute the same function but serve different purposes. predict() is an inference utility: it splits the data into batches, runs each batch, converts results to NumPy and concatenates them. That conversion leaves the framework's autodiff system, so no gradient can flow back through it. model(x) is a direct, in-memory call on backend tensors, and the backend can record and differentiate it. Here we need d(loss)/d(image), so the feature extractor must be called as feature_extractor(image), which is exactly what compute_loss does.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Using predict() inside a GradientTape is a common bug. The tape sees a NumPy array, so tape.gradient returns None, or the code fails outright. The opposite mistake, calling model(x) on a huge dataset, can run out of memory, because it processes everything in one pass with no batching.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Differentiability requires that every operation between the watched input and the loss be a backend tensor op. predict() breaks that chain by materializing NumPy outputs.

terminology.meaning: Direct call of a Keras model on a tensor; runs eagerly or inside a traced function and is differentiable.
Batched inference loop that returns NumPy arrays; scalable but not differentiable.

connections: p.317: the first part of this sidebar explains that predict() loops over batches and extracts NumPy values, and is not differentiable
p.91: GradientTape records operations on tensors, which is why the model must be called directly

paragraphs.excerpt: A non-obvious trick to help the gradient-ascent process go smoothly is to normalize
paragraphs.what_it_says: Divide the gradient tensor by its L2 norm (the square root of the sum of the squares of its values). This keeps the magnitude of the updates to the input image within the same range.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The raw gradient of a filter's mean activation with respect to the pixels can have very different sizes from step to step, from filter to filter and from layer to layer. Some filters barely react to a gray image, so the gradient is tiny; others react strongly, so it is huge. Dividing by the norm keeps only the direction of steepest ascent and throws away the scale. The learning rate then sets the actual step length: each update has L2 length close to the learning rate. This is similar in spirit to normalized gradient descent and to the sign-based steps used in adversarial attacks.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without normalization, one learning rate would not work across all the filters the visualization loop on p.320 will process. It would overshoot for some filters and stall for others. With normalization, a single learning_rate value behaves predictably.
paragraphs.technical_idea: g_normalized = g / ||g||_2. The update x <- x + eta * g_normalized then has norm eta, regardless of how large g was.

terminology.meaning: Euclidean length of a tensor seen as one long vector: sqrt(sum of squared entries).
Rescaling a gradient to unit norm so that only its direction is used.

connections: p.319: the line grads = ops.normalize(grads) applies this trick in all three backend versions
p.320: the visualization loop uses one fixed learning rate for every filter, which relies on this normalization

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s set up the gradient ascent step function. Anything that involves gradients requires calling
paragraphs.what_it_says: The next step is the gradient-ascent step function. Any computation involving gradients needs backend-level APIs: GradientTape in TensorFlow, .backward() in PyTorch, jax.grad() in JAX. The authors show the snippet for all three backends, starting with TensorFlow.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Keras 3 abstracts the forward computation (keras.ops works on any backend), but it has no backend-agnostic API for 'give me the gradient of this with respect to that'. Each framework has its own autodiff design. TensorFlow records operations on a tape. PyTorch builds a dynamic graph and accumulates .grad on leaf tensors. JAX transforms a pure function into its gradient function. So the step function is the one place in this example where backend-specific code is unavoidable.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Readers learn to separate backend-agnostic parts (model, compute_loss, ops.normalize) from backend-specific parts (the gradient call). This is the same split as the custom training loops in chapter 7.

terminology.meaning: The low-level framework (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX) on which Keras 3 executes.
Moving parameters (here, pixels) in the direction of the gradient to increase a quantity rather than decrease it.

connections: p.91: TensorFlow GradientTape introduced in chapter 3
p.110: JAX's metaprogramming approach with jax.grad()
p.240: the same per-backend split appears for custom training steps in chapter 7

paragraphs.excerpt: For TensorFlow, we can just open a `GradientTape` scope and compute the loss
paragraphs.what_it_says: In TensorFlow, open a GradientTape scope, compute the loss inside it, and retrieve the gradients. A @tf.function decorator speeds up the computation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Operations run inside the `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` block are recorded. After the block, tape.gradient(loss, image) walks the recording backwards with the chain rule. @tf.function traces the Python function once into a TensorFlow graph and reuses it on later calls. That avoids Python overhead on each of the many gradient-ascent iterations.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The visualization loop calls the step function many times per filter and repeats this for many filters. Graph compilation makes this much faster.
paragraphs.technical_idea: tf.function retraces when the input signature changes (for example a new Python value for filter_index). Beyond the book: passing filter_index as a Python int can trigger a retrace for each new filter, while passing a tensor avoids it.

terminology.meaning: TensorFlow context manager that records operations so gradients can be computed afterwards.
Decorator that compiles a Python function into a TensorFlow graph for faster repeated execution.

connections: p.80: GradientTape first used in chapter 2 to compute weight gradients
p.240: a tf.function-compiled training step in chapter 7

concepts.name: Gradient ascent in input space
concepts.definition: Optimizing the input of a fixed, trained network (here, image pixels) to maximize some internal or output quantity, by repeatedly stepping in the direction of that quantity's gradient with respect to the input.
concepts.intuition: Instead of asking 'which weights fit the data?', we ask 'which image would make this filter fire as strongly as possible?' The network is frozen; the image is what we train.
concepts.technical: Given a loss L(x) = mean activation of filter f, iterate x_{t+1} = x_t + eta * grad_x L(x_t) / ||grad_x L(x_t)||_2. The gradient is computed by backpropagating through the feature extractor down to the input tensor.
concepts.significance: This is the basis for filter visualization (this section), DeepDream, style transfer and adversarial examples.
concepts.example: Start from a gray-ish noisy 200x200 image (p.320) and, over about 30 steps, it turns into a texture of the stripes or dots that filter 2 of block3_sepconv1 detects.
concepts.misconception: It is not training: no model weight changes. Only the input tensor is updated.

concepts.name: L2 gradient normalization
concepts.definition: Dividing a gradient tensor by its L2 norm so that it has unit length, keeping only its direction.
concepts.intuition: The gradient says which way is uphill. Its length depends on how steep the slope is right now, which can vary enormously. Normalizing means 'always take a step of the same size uphill'.
concepts.technical: g_hat = g / sqrt(sum_i g_i^2). In practice a small epsilon is added to the denominator to avoid division by zero when the gradient vanishes.
concepts.significance: It makes a single learning rate work across filters and layers whose activation scales differ, and it prevents explosive or stalled updates.
concepts.example: g = (3, 4) has norm 5, so g_hat = (0.6, 0.8). With learning rate 10 the pixels move by (6, 8), whatever the original gradient size was.
concepts.misconception: Normalization does not change the direction of ascent, so it does not 'distort' the optimization; it changes only the step length.

concepts.name: GradientTape
concepts.definition: TensorFlow's autodiff API: a context manager that records operations on watched tensors and can then return gradients of a result with respect to them.
concepts.intuition: Think of it as a tape recorder for math. Press record, do the computation, then play the recording backwards to get derivatives.
concepts.technical: Trainable tf.Variables are watched automatically. Plain tensors (like the image here) must be registered with tape.watch(tensor). Gradients are retrieved with tape.gradient(target, sources).
concepts.significance: It is the TensorFlow route to any custom gradient computation in Keras 3 when the backend is TensorFlow.
concepts.example: with tf.GradientTape() as tape: tape.watch(image); loss = compute_loss(image, 2); grads = tape.gradient(loss, image).
concepts.misconception: Forgetting tape.watch on a non-Variable tensor does not raise an error. tape.gradient simply returns None.

concepts.name: Feature extractor model
concepts.definition: A Keras Model built with the functional API whose output is an intermediate layer's output of a pretrained network.
concepts.intuition: It cuts the network at a chosen layer and exposes what that layer 'sees'.
concepts.technical: keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output) reuses the pretrained layers and weights up to block3_sepconv1; it returns a tensor of shape (batch, height, width, channels) for that layer.
concepts.significance: It lets compute_loss read individual filter activations and differentiate them with respect to the input.
concepts.example: feature_extractor(image)[:, :, :, 2] is the activation map of filter 2.
concepts.misconception: It does not copy the weights; it shares the same layer objects as the original model.

concepts.name: model(x) vs model.predict(x)
concepts.definition: Two ways to run a Keras model: a direct differentiable call on tensors, and a batched, NumPy-returning, non-differentiable inference loop.
concepts.intuition: model(x) is a calculator you can take derivatives through; predict() is a factory line that turns out finished NumPy results.
concepts.technical: predict() iterates in batches (batch_size argument) and converts outputs to NumPy, which leaves the autodiff graph. model(x) stays in backend tensors.
concepts.significance: Choosing the wrong one either breaks gradient computation or exhausts memory.
concepts.example: Inside gradient_ascent_step: feature_extractor(image). For extracting features from 10,000 images: feature_extractor.predict(images, batch_size=64).
concepts.misconception: They do not compute different functions; the outputs are numerically the same. Only differentiability and scalability differ.

math.title: L2 norm of the gradient and the normalized gradient
math.source_text: normalize the gradient tensor by dividing it by its L2 norm (the square root of the sum of the squares of the values in the tensor)

variables.meaning: Gradient of the loss with respect to the input image, a tensor of the same shape as the image; treated as one long vector.
One entry of the gradient (one channel of one pixel).
Normalized gradient, with unit L2 norm.

math.operations: Square every entry, sum them all, take the square root, then divide every entry by that number.
math.purpose: To make the update magnitude independent of how large the raw gradient happens to be.
math.interpretation: \hat g points in the same direction as g (steepest ascent) but always has length 1.
math.intuition: Like keeping a compass bearing and ignoring how steep the hill is.
math.numerical_example: If $g = (3, -4, 0, 12)$ then $\lVert g \rVert_2 = \sqrt{9+16+0+144} = 13$ and $\hat g = (0.231, -0.308, 0, 0.923)$, whose length is 1. Beyond the book: if $g$ were 1000 times larger, $\hat g$ would be identical.

math.title: Normalized gradient-ascent update
math.source_text: grads = ops.normalize(grads); image += learning_rate * grads (completed on p.319)

variables.meaning: compute_loss: mean activation of the chosen filter.
Gradient of the loss with respect to the image pixels.

math.operations: Compute the gradient, normalize it, scale by the learning rate, and add it to the image (plus sign = ascent).
math.purpose: To increase the filter's activation by a controlled amount at each step.
math.interpretation: With an exactly L2-normalized gradient each step moves the image by Euclidean distance eta. Beyond the book: Keras' ops.normalize normalizes along the last axis by default, so in the code each pixel's channel vector is normalized separately (see p.319).
math.intuition: Gradient descent with the sign flipped and a fixed stride.

math.title: The filter-activation loss (border excluded)

variables.meaning: Activation of filter f at spatial position (i, j) for batch element b, output of block3_sepconv1.
Batch size and spatial height/width of the layer's activation map.

math.operations: Slice off 2 rows/columns at each border, select channel f, average everything that remains.
math.purpose: A scalar measure of how strongly the image activates filter f, which gradient ascent maximizes.
math.interpretation: Excluding the borders (p.317's callout: 'We avoid border artifacts') stops the optimization from exploiting padding effects at the image edges.
math.intuition: The average 'excitement' of one feature detector over the interior of the image.

code.title: Shared setup: Xception feature extractor and compute_loss (recap)
code.original_code:
import keras
import keras_hub
from keras import ops

model = keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")

layer_name = "block3_sepconv1"
layer = model.get_layer(name=layer_name)
feature_extractor = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output)

def compute_loss(image, filter_index):
    activation = feature_extractor(image)
    filter_activation = activation[:, 2:-2, 2:-2, filter_index]
    return ops.mean(filter_activation)
code.what_it_does: Collects the backend-agnostic pieces that the three backend-specific step functions share. It loads the ImageNet-pretrained Xception backbone, builds a model that outputs the activations of layer block3_sepconv1, and defines a loss that is the mean activation of one filter of that layer.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports Keras, KerasHub (pretrained model presets) and keras.ops, the backend-agnostic tensor operations namespace.
Loads the Xception backbone (convolutional base without classifier head) with ImageNet weights from the preset xception_41_imagenet.
Chooses the separable convolution layer block3_sepconv1, an early-to-mid layer, and retrieves it by name.
Functional API: a new Model mapping the backbone's input to that layer's output, sharing the pretrained weights.
compute_loss runs the feature extractor directly (model(x)-style, differentiable, as the sidebar requires).
Selects channel filter_index and drops 2 pixels on each spatial border to avoid border artifacts (as stated on p.317).
Returns a scalar: the mean of the remaining activations. This is the quantity gradient ascent will maximize.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: an image tensor of shape (batch, height, width, 3), already preprocessed to Xception's range, and an integer filter index. Output of compute_loss: a scalar tensor.
code.algorithm: Forward pass to an intermediate layer, then slicing and averaging to reduce one feature map to a scalar objective.
code.theory_link: The loss must be a scalar for its gradient to have the same shape as the input. Averaging gives a smooth objective in which every interior position contributes.

parameters.name: layer_name
parameters.role: Which layer's filters to visualize; deeper layers give more complex patterns (p.321-322).

parameters.name: filter_index
parameters.role: Which channel of that layer the loss measures.
Border crop width on each side.

pitfalls: Calling feature_extractor.predict(image) inside compute_loss would break differentiation.
Forgetting the model-specific preprocessing makes the activations meaningless; p.317 applies the preprocessor first.
Beyond the book: the layer name must match the preset's naming; use model.summary() to list layer names.

Opens the tape: operations executed in this block are recorded.

code.algorithm: One step of normalized gradient ascent on the input.
code.theory_link: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation: the tape records the forward graph from image to loss so it can be traversed backward.

pitfalls: Without tape.watch(image), tape.gradient(loss, image) returns None because the image is a plain tensor, not a Variable.
tape.watch must be called before the loss is computed, inside the with block.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written sketch (not from the book): what goes wrong without watch
import tensorflow as tf
x = tf.constant(3.0)
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    y = x * x
print(tape.gradient(y, x))  # None
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    tape.watch(x)
    y = x * x
print(tape.gradient(y, x))  # tf.Tensor(6.0)

deeper.title: Why the gradient's size is unreliable
deeper.body:
The size of $\nabla_x \mathcal{L}$ depends on many things that have nothing to do with how good the current update direction is:

- **The filter**: some filters have large weights or sit after high-variance activations.
- **The current image**: at a random start the filter may be nearly inactive. If its activations are mostly in the zero region of a ReLU-like nonlinearity, the gradient is tiny. As the pattern emerges, the gradient can grow quickly.
- **The layer depth**: gradients that pass through many layers can shrink or grow.

Normalizing strips all of this away. Beyond the book: the same idea appears in DeepDream implementations and in the Fast Gradient Sign Method for adversarial examples, which keeps only the sign of each gradient entry.

deeper.title: Analogy: walking uphill in fog
deeper.body: Imagine climbing a hill in thick fog with a slope meter. On gentle ground a raw-gradient rule would have you shuffle a few millimeters; near a cliff it would make you leap a kilometer. Normalized gradient ascent says: read the direction of steepest climb, then always take a one-meter stride. You progress steadily whatever the terrain, and the stride length (the learning rate) is the only knob.

deeper.title: Where the three backends differ
deeper.body:
| Backend | How the gradient is obtained | What you must remember |
|---|---|---|
| TensorFlow | `GradientTape` records ops; `tape.gradient(loss, image)` | `tape.watch(image)` for non-Variables |
| PyTorch | `loss.backward()` fills `image.grad` | the image must have `requires_grad=True` (p.319) |
| JAX | `jax.grad(compute_loss)` returns a gradient function | the loss function must be pure, and the image must be its first argument (p.110) |

The compile decorators are also backend-specific: `@tf.function` (TensorFlow) and `@jax.jit` (JAX, p.319). The PyTorch version on p.319 runs eagerly.

misconceptions.claim: model.predict(x) and model(x) give different outputs.
misconceptions.correction: They compute the same function. predict() is batched and returns NumPy, so it scales but is not differentiable; model(x) is in-memory and differentiable.

misconceptions.claim: GradientTape automatically tracks every tensor used inside it.
misconceptions.correction: Only trainable Variables are watched automatically. A constant or plain tensor such as the input image needs tape.watch(image), as the callout on Listing 10.11 says.

misconceptions.claim: Normalizing the gradient changes the direction the image moves in.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing by a positive scalar (the L2 norm) preserves direction and only fixes the step length.

misconceptions.claim: Filter visualization retrains the network on a new image.
misconceptions.correction: The weights stay frozen. Only the input pixels are updated, to maximize one filter's activation.

Normalize the gradient by its L2 norm so each update has a consistent magnitude.

questions.question: Why must compute_loss call feature_extractor(image) rather than feature_extractor.predict(image)?
options: predict() is not differentiable, so gradients cannot flow back to the image
predict() cannot handle a batch of one image
predict() does not apply the model's weights
questions.answer: predict() is not differentiable, so gradients cannot flow back to the image
questions.explanation: The sidebar (p.317-318) says predict() extracts NumPy values batch by batch and cannot be backpropagated through. The outputs are the same, so the first option is wrong. predict() handles any batch size, so the third is wrong. It certainly uses the weights, so the fourth is wrong.

questions.question: A gradient tensor has entries (2, -1, 2). Compute its L2 norm and the normalized gradient. With learning_rate = 10, how far (in L2 distance) does the image move?
questions.answer: Norm = sqrt(4+1+4) = 3; normalized gradient = (0.667, -0.333, 0.667); the image moves by 10 * 1 = 10 in L2 distance.
questions.explanation: The L2 norm is the square root of the sum of squares (p.318). Dividing by it gives a unit vector, so the update learning_rate * g_hat has norm exactly learning_rate.

questions.question: What does tape.watch(image) do in Listing 10.11, and what would happen without it?
questions.answer: It tells the GradientTape to record operations involving the image tensor. Without it, the image (not a Variable) is not tracked and tape.gradient(loss, image) returns None.
questions.explanation: The callout says only Variables are watched automatically. p.91 explains the same rule for constant tensors.

questions.question: Why does gradient normalization make it easier to use one learning rate for every filter in the visualization loop?
questions.answer: Raw gradient magnitudes differ widely between filters and between steps. After normalization only the direction remains, so the learning rate alone sets the step size, and the same value behaves similarly for every filter.
questions.explanation: The page says normalization ensures update magnitudes stay within the same range. That is exactly what makes a shared hyperparameter workable.

questions.question: Which statement about compute_loss is correct?
options: It returns the class probability for ImageNet class filter_index
It returns the mean activation of one channel of block3_sepconv1, excluding a 2-pixel border
It returns the sum of all channels of the last Xception layer
It returns the crossentropy between the image and a target pattern
questions.answer: It returns the mean activation of one channel of block3_sepconv1, excluding a 2-pixel border
questions.explanation: The code slices activation[:, 2:-2, 2:-2, filter_index] from the block3_sepconv1 feature extractor and takes ops.mean. The backbone has no classifier head, nothing sums all channels, and no crossentropy is involved.

questions.question: Name the gradient API used by each of the three backends, according to this page.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph introducing the step function.

questions.explanation: Compare with Listing 10.11 (p.318-319). Check that you remembered tape.watch and why it is needed.
